function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

### The “best” city for an ice‑hockey‑focused trip to Iceland? **Reykjavík** – the capital and the hub of Iceland’s hockey scene. | Why Reykjavík stands out | What you’ll find there | |---------------------------|------------------------| | **Largest and most modern rink** – *Íshús Reykjavíkur* (Ice Hall) is the home of the national team and hosts the Icelandic Hockey League’s biggest games. | • 2‑rink complex (one 200 m², one 100 m²).
• 1,200‑seat spectator capacity.
• Ice‑maintenance tech, lighting, and a full‑size scoreboard. | | **National team & league action** – The Icelandic Hockey League (IHL) plays its regular season and playoffs here. | • Regular season games (Oct‑Mar).
• Playoffs & finals (Mar‑Apr).
• National team training camps in summer. | | **Community & culture** – Reykjavík’s hockey community is tight‑knit, with youth programs, adult leagues, and a strong fan base. | • Youth clinics (U‑12, U‑16).
• Adult “social” leagues (Saturday nights).
• Fan‑friendly bars and cafés that show game highlights. | | **Convenient travel & amenities** – The city offers the best transport links, accommodation options, and a vibrant nightlife. | • International airport (Keflavík).
• Hotels ranging from boutique to budget.
• Restaurants, museums, and the famous Hallgrímskirkja church. | --- ## Other Icelandic cities worth a visit if you’re into ice hockey | City | Highlights | When to go | |------|------------|------------| | **Akureyri** | • *Akureyri Ice Rink* – the second‑largest rink in Iceland.
• Home to the *Akureyri Hockey Club* (AIC).
• Friendly local league games. | • Regular season (Oct‑Mar).
• Summer training camps. | | **Húsavík** | • Small but passionate community rink.
• Occasionally hosts exhibition matches. | • Late summer/early fall for community events. | | **Kópavogur** | • *Kópavogur Ice Rink* – good for casual play and youth leagues. | • Year‑round, especially during school holidays. | --- ## Planning Your Trip | Tip | Detail | |-----|--------| | **Book early for league games** | IHL games sell out quickly, especially the playoffs. Check the official IHL website or the *Íshús Reykjavíkur* calendar. | | **Combine hockey with Icelandic culture** | After a game, explore Reykjavík’s museums (National Museum, Saga Museum), try local cuisine (skyr, lamb, seafood), and enjoy the nightlife. | | **Weather gear** | Even in summer, temperatures can dip below 0 °C at night. Pack layers, waterproof jackets, and gloves. | | **Transport** | Reykjavík’s public bus system (Strætó) runs to the ice hall. Taxis and rideshare apps are plentiful. | | **Accommodation** | For a hockey‑centric stay, consider hotels near the ice hall (e.g., Hotel Borg, Radisson Blu). For budget travelers, hostels like Kex Hostel offer dorms and a lively atmosphere. | | **Language** | English is widely spoken, especially in the sports community. A few Icelandic phrases (“Halló!” – Hello, “Takk!” – Thank you) go a long way. | --- ## Quick FAQ | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Is Iceland a big ice‑hockey country?** | No, hockey is a niche sport, but the national team competes in the IIHF World Championships (Division I). The passion is strong, and the facilities are top‑notch. | | **Can I watch a live game?** | Yes. The IHL season runs Oct‑Mar, with playoffs in Mar‑Apr. Check the schedule on the IHL or *Íshús Reykjavíkur* websites. | | **Are there opportunities to play?** | Absolutely! Many rinks host open‑practice sessions, youth clinics, and adult social leagues. | | **What’s the best time to visit?** | Late summer (Aug‑Sep) for mild weather and fewer crowds, or winter (Dec‑Feb) for a true Nordic experience (though the rink will be in full operation). | --- ### Bottom line If you’re looking for the richest ice‑hockey experience in Iceland—top‑class rinks, national team action, and a vibrant local community—**Reykjavík** is your go‑to city. For a more intimate, community‑driven vibe, consider **Akureyri**. Either way, you’ll get a taste of Icelandic hockey culture, plus the chance to explore the country’s stunning landscapes and unique heritage. Enjoy the game—and the adventure!
